pr_title: Make PriorityQueue near FIFO for same priority Pods by leveraging Pod creation time
pr_body:
**What type of PR is this?**
/kind bug

**What this PR does / why we need it**:
See https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/83834 and https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/83826

**Which issue(s) this PR fixes**:
Fixes https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/83834
Fixes https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/83826
PartOfLongTermFinalSolutionFor https://github.com/microsoft/pai/issues/3704


**Special notes for your reviewer**:

**Does this PR introduce a user-facing change?**:
yes
```release-note
Make PriorityQueue near FIFO for same priority Pods by leveraging Pod creation time

issue_context.title: PriorityQueue is far from FIFO for same priority Pods
issue_context.body:
<!-- Please use this template while reporting a bug and provide as much info as possible. Not doing so may result in your bug not being addressed in a timely manner. Thanks!

If the matter is security related, please disclose it privately via https://kubernetes.io/security/
-->


**What happened**:
By default, user Pod does not have priority (i.e. 0), so usually, they expect **FIFO** scheduling in this case, even if for the PriorityQueue.
In this requirement, the **FI(First In)** should be determined by the [Pod CreationTimestamp instead of last queued time](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/83826), i.e. the **user expect longest Pending Pod since creation should be scheduled first in most cases**.
However, we found that the PriorityQueue is far from FIFO, i.e. >40% Pods cut in line, see **How to reproduce it** for more details.

**What you expected to happen**:
The PriorityQueue should be **near FIFO** for same priority Pods, i.e. <5% Pods cut in line.

**How to reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)**:
1. Cluster Setup: 7 Nodes each has 4 total free GPUs
2. Submit ReplicaSet RSX, which contains 28 Pods, and each Pod request 1 GPU and just sleep forever in its command.
3. Wait all Pods in RSX is running.
4. Submit Job JA, which contains 200 Pods to run to complete, and each Pod request 1 GPU and just sleep 20s in its command.
5. Wait all Pods in JA is queued in scheduler. (Because no free GPUs, so all Pods in JA are pending)
6. Submit Job JB, which has the same spec with JA except for its name JB is different with JA. (Here, we ensures JB is totally later than JA)
7. Delete ReplicaSet RSX, so JA and JB will compete to schedule.

We obeserves below result consistently:
| Timestamp (normalized) | JA completed Pods | JB completed Pods| Pods cut in line rate|
|:---- |:---- |:---- |:---- |
| 1 | 72 | 56 | 56/200 |
| 2 | 108 | 76 | 76/200 |
| 3 | 138 | 101 | 101/200 |
| 4 | 169 | 131 | 131/200 |
| 5 | 182 | 153 | 153/200 |
In avarage, >40% Pods cut in line.

**Anything else we need to know?**:
This issue can be fixed, i.e. cut in line rate decreased <5%, after we used the **Pod creation time instead of the last queued time to sort Pod for the same priority**, as suggested in https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/83826, and fixed by https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/83835.

After the fix https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/83835, we obeserves below result consistently (for the same repro steps above):
| Timestamp (normalized) | JA completed Pods | JB completed Pods| Pods cut in line rate|
|:---- |:---- |:---- |:---- |
| 1 | 160 | 1| 1/200 |
| 2 | 181 | 1| 1/200 |
| 3 | 191 | 3| 3/200 |
| 4 | 194 | 21| 21/200 |
In avarage, <5% Pods cut in line.


**Environment**:
- Kubernetes version (use `kubectl version`):
```
Client Version: version.Info{Major:"1", Minor:"13", GitVersion:"v1.13.4", GitCommit:"c27b913fddd1a6c480c229191a087698aa92f0b1", GitTreeState:"clean", BuildDate:"2019-02-28T13:37:52Z", GoVersion:"go1.11.5", Compiler:"gc", Platform:"linux/amd64"}
Server Version: version.Info{Major:"1", Minor:"14", GitVersion:"v1.14.2", GitCommit:"66049e3b21efe110454d67df4fa62b08ea79a19b", GitTreeState:"clean", BuildDate:"2019-05-16T16:14:56Z", GoVersion:"go1.12.5", Compiler:"gc", Platform:"linux/amd64"}
```
- Scheduler Spec:
```

metadata:
  name: kube-scheduler
  namespace: kube-system
spec:
  hostNetwork: true
  containers:
  - image: gcr.io/google_containers/kube-scheduler:v1.14.2
    name: kube-scheduler
    command:
    - /usr/local/bin/kube-scheduler

    - 10.151.41.16:8080

    livenessProbe:

/sig scheduling
@bsalamat and @denkensk PTAL

We came cross similar problem. 

> cut in line rate decreased <5%

How to guarantee it? Suppose that JA's pods are all in back off queue, and there are available GPU resource, then all JB's pods will be scheduled.

I cannot guarantee this, this is just a rough estimation for this specific reproduce steps.

> Suppose that JA's pods are all in back off queue, and there are available GPU resource, then all JB's pods will be scheduled.

Anyway, the probability for your case should be very small, because even if in current sort policy, JA and JB is **expected** to share the active queue evenly. And after #83835, JA is **expected** to contains more Pods in active queue than JB.

What user really care is the **expectation (average case)** of the cut in line rate instead of the **worst case** to guarantee, and #83835 's goal is to reduce the former.

BTW, it need some mathematical calculations to get the [expectation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Expected_value) of the cut in line rate, but we definitely know that it must be less than current sort policy.
/priority important-soon

In your example, it seems like the cluster is getting less work done after your change?

| 4 | 169 | 131 | 131/200 |
versus
| 4 | 194 | 21| 21/200 |

300 jobs done > 215 jobs done, so your throughput is better before the change

Do jobs A and B have ordering requirements with each other?

@riking  Note the Timestamp in the table is normalized, which means one specific value only have relative meaning in its own table. From what I tested, the throughout looks the same before and after this change.
Job A and Job B doesn't depend on each other, this issue just wants to tell that they are queued in an unfair way.

Maybe this was asked before, but, if so, better resurface those conclusions in this issue.

Why should the scheduler be near FIFO? If a user comes in with a lot of jobs, they will almost completely starve other users that would come later. It is not like that in modern operating systems. Instead, I believe our current strategy tries to be more responsive to new jobs.

@alculquicondor it don't have to be like this, anyway we are searching a possibility to configure it this way for some use cases.
eg. a limited nb of available nodes and a large number of jobs coming in that needs to provide a answer as fast as possible regarding their arriving time.
Seems when no explicit defined policies to judge the priority of 2 tasks (such as priority field, user max tasks limit, etc), the FIFO rule can be the default policy which meets most human sense.

Again, near FIFO is not how most operating systems work today. I don't think that would be the user expectation. I would like to know more arguments, given that you suggest that FIFO should be the default.
Pls check this https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/83835#discussion_r335299603

That seems reasonable as an argument to have an alternate behavior, but not to make it the default.

Personally, I think FIFO is a greater source of starvation. And that is why operating systems schedulers moved away from it to be more responsive to all users. But if I understand correctly, the appeal is coming from batch-type jobs. So maybe a better solution for it is co-scheduling, for which a KEP is in review: kubernetes/enhancements#1463

Possible courses of action:

- Work on a queue sort plugin on https://github.com/kubernetes-sigs/scheduler-plugins
- Write a KEP that would explain the motivation and use cases.

We have already solved the co-scheduling/gang-scheduling problem by scheduler extender.
However:
For job requires gang-scheduling, non-FIFO still impacts among these jobs (pod groups).
For job does not require gang-scheduling, non-FIFO not only impact among these jobs, but also impacts among their pods.

Besides, to be FIFO, does not have to sacrifice too much responsive or utilization, see my proposal in #86373.

BTW, if we do not respect FIFO, in theory, it can still cause starvation. Because the early pod may be scheduled later than later pod, so it may not be scheduled forever.
What I mean is that, it is not FIFO that cause starvation, it is current K8S **implementation** (priority queue + backoff queue), that to be FIFO is more easy to cause starvation.
And even without FIFO, as current implementation, K8S still has starvation as #86373 said.
If we totally solved #86373, to be FIFO should be acceptable. Because FIFO is equivalent to pods with different priorities, if latter doesn't have starvation anymore, former also doesn't.

> We have already solved the co-scheduling/gang-scheduling problem by scheduler extender.

Note that the KEP is also using the queuesort endpoint. Extenders can't do that.

> BTW, if we do not respect FIFO, in theory, it can still cause starvation. Because the early pod may be scheduled later than later pod, so it may not be scheduled forever.

An earlier pod will eventually have an earlier timestamp. Quoting Bobby again:

> The existing logic of sorting based on last schedule attempt timestamp is fair. If we sorted pods with the same priority by their creation time, an unschedulable pod created earlier than others would get more scheduling cycles than other pods with the same priority.

I'm trying to advocate for policy more than implementation. The implementation had issues with backoffs that we have fixed for 1.18, although there is still #87850 which is awaiting for experiments. I believe this is the last piece to solve HOL blocking.

> Because FIFO is equivalent to pods with different priorities, if latter doesn't have starvation anymore, former also doesn't.

This is true, but dangerous. We are basically saying that earlier pods have higher priority. Even if there is no HOL, responsiveness for new pods will be affected.

Other than that, I think your proposed algorithm in #86373 has one problem. As I understand, unschedulable pods are inserted back to the queue after each cycle. If there are too many unschedulable pods with higher priority or early creation time, the throughput of the scheduler is reduced. Because the scheduler has to retry those pods before moving to the newer pods that might fit.

But now we are talking about two problems in two different threads. I think we need a KEP or a doc with your proposal so that we can more easily comment on specific aspects.

> I believe this is the last piece to solve HOL blocking.

Actually, it's not the last piece. We could try to be more diligent identifying the events that bring pods from the unschedulable queue back into the scheduling queue. But that is a bigger effort with too many corner cases, whereas #87850 is more low-hanging.

Extender can do gang scheduling, because in our setup, the pods in the same group shares the same priority (with job creation time encoded) with the whole job. So even without queue sort plugin, and with our gang reservation, all pods in the group will eventually (normally very fast in fact) fill to the reservation and get allocated.

BTW, I avoid to compare k8s with modern OS, because OS is so different than current k8s, for example, the preemption in OS, normally just suspend process, instead of killing it, while K8S preemption is killing. So OS can switch to different process without too much hurts, but k8s cannot. So k8s needs to take more care to select which pod to run now. If the later pod is selected, then the early pod may have to wait until it complete. If then another later pod2 is selected, early pod may also need to wait pod2. This is not intuitive for users.

Sorry to diverge from the root debate but does anyone of you can help implementing a workaround to create a FIFO QueueSort plugin on Scheduler Framework with out-of-tree feature (https://github.com/kubernetes/enhancements/blob/master/keps/sig-scheduling/20180409-scheduling-framework.md#custom-scheduler-plugins-out-of-tree) ?

As I am not familiar Scheduler Framework, it seems that I need to compile a full Scheduler, and that I have to write it in Golang only.
Documentation is very light on this topic, and I can't find any clear example on how to make & deploy such a plugin.
Does anyone have a link with a clear how-to about such task (out-of-tree technique) ?

Basically the less() function using K8S Go SDK looks easy to implement, it's more about deploying the plugin onto/with the Scheduler.

Thanks a lot for you help.

--

EDIT 1
The best example I found yet is https://sysdig.com/blog/kubernetes-scheduler/ but it's not using Scheduler Framework at all, anyway it has the advantage to be developed in Python that is more familiar to me.

EDIT 2
Well I will go with https://kubernetes.io/docs/tasks/administer-cluster/configure-multiple-schedulers/ to add an extra scheduler, maybe then I will be able to use out-of-tree technique

The framework is quite new and we are only fully leveraging it in 1.18. In the future, we would like to have a sample in https://github.com/kubernetes-sigs/scheduler-plugins
That is indeed the doc to set it up https://kubernetes.io/docs/tasks/administer-cluster/configure-multiple-schedulers once you have the code. But better use the mailing list or slack channel if you have further questions.

> I avoid to compare k8s with modern OS, because OS is so different than current k8s

The truth is that different users will always have a different view of their clusters. Following with the OS comparison, there are specialized schedulers for RT needs.

The current behavior follows a multi-user environment were we try to avoid a single deployment (as a concept, not necessarily a `apps/v1.Deployment`) from overtaking the cluster. And this is useful if several services are trying to scale up at roughly the same time. It seems that your view is more of a batch environment were a job should finish before another one is allowed to start. Unless there is enough space for both.

Changing a default behavior is not an easy task and it requires to follow release and deprecation policies. Users might be relying on it.

But, that doesn't prevent us to add new optional behaviors. And this is simpler with the framework. We just need a KEP :)

Agree! It is hard or impossible to make single scheduler sutiable for all scenarios.
BTW, for the first step, we can clarify current scheduler behavior, such as not FIFO, in our wiki:
https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/configuration/pod-priority-preemption/#effect-of-pod-priority-on-scheduling-order

review_comments: This is a not a good idea. The existing logic of sorting based on last schedule attempt timestamp is fair. If we sorted pods with the same priority by their creation time, an unschedulable pod created earlier than others would get more scheduling cycles than other pods with the same priority.

Thanks for the review :)

> If we sorted pods with the same priority by their creation time, an unschedulable pod created earlier than others would get more scheduling cycles than other pods with the same priority.

I knew this, and this is the **key goal** of this PR.

To judge whether this PR is a good idea, i.e. fair, **we would better ask our end users** of the scheduler: "if it is fair for them".

For example, for a cluster whose capacity only can serves 2 running pods at a time. UserA's JobA has 3 concurrent pods to run to complete, and each pod need to run **2hrs**, UserB's Job B has the same spec with JobA but submitted **1hrs** later, UserC's JobC has the same spec with JobB but submitted 1hrs later,..., until JobZ.

So, current scheduler logic gives nearly the same scheduling cycles for JobA, JobB...JobZ. JobA is likely to wait until JobB even JobZ to finish. So, UserA will certainly feel that current scheduler logic is very **unfair** for him (the same for UserB...UserY), because **people in our society already built a consensus that first coming first serving, they generally cannot tolerate other people cut in line.**

See more in:
https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cutting_in_line
> The act, which may be **taboo** in some instances, stands in stark contrast to the **normal** policy of first come, first served that governs **most** queue areas.

And what I mentioned in https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/83834:

> By default, user Pod does not have priority (i.e. 0), so usually, they expect **FIFO** scheduling in this case, even if for the PriorityQueue.
> In this requirement, the **FI(First In)** should be determined by the [Pod CreationTimestamp instead of last queued time](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/83826), i.e. the **user expect longest Pending Pod since creation should be scheduled first in most cases**.
> However, we found that the PriorityQueue is far from FIFO, i.e. >40% Pods cut in line, see **How to reproduce it** for more details.


And what I mentioned in https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/83826:

> And even if the scheduler is not re-informed by restarting etc, using last queued time still causes https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/83834. And the reason is that after a Pod is poped for scheduling and then added back to queue again, its **last queued time** is updated to now (above `newPodInfo `is called again). So, if still sort by the time, it is no longer represent the **Pod pending time since created**, it just represent the **Pod pending time since last scheduled** which **user does not aware and does not care**, they just know the former Pod pending time.

What do you think about this?
How shall we define "what is **fair**"?
Thanks

After the scheduling framework is ready, you could customize the scheduler behavior with the queue-sort extension point. But I think it would be better for us to maintain the current behavior which we used for quite a while.

@draveness Thanks for this info, great extension point!
Some questions related:
1. Can we make the "near FIFO (sort by creation time)" as a **built-in** policy, since it is a too common requirement? So we just need to tune config to make it work in clould, such as AKS.

2. I know current behavior is used for quite a while. But it **should not be the reason to block us to rethink** "is it reasonable, i.e. fair for our users". As we switch the default queue from FIFOQueue to PriorityQueue, we can also switch the **default queuing policy** for PriorityQueue to be "near FIFO (sort by creation time)", if it is more reasonable. Anyway, switch to more reasonable **default policy** is better than insist the unreasonable one forever.

Thanks

> I know current behavior is used for quite a while. But it should not be the reason to block us to rethink "is it reasonable, i.e. fair" for our users?

Agreed, we could have the discussion at https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/83834. And I'd like to hear what Bobby thinks of this. Why did we make the decisions to sort pod by last queue time instead of creation timestamp? :)

It is already a FIFO for the pods that have never been tried before (and have the same priority). The first time "queue time" is creation time, but in subsequent retries, we use the time that a pod is added to the queue. This is roughly the same as the last scheduler retry. Why should a pod that is created earlier go to the head of the queue in all the retries? This would be unfair to other pods with the same priority.

Imagine this scenario, pods are created in this order:

queue: 1, 2, 3, 4, 5
If we implemented the algorithm proposed in this PR, the scheduler picks 1 and tries. It is unschedulable. It picks 2 and puts 1 back. The queue will look:

queue: 1, 3, 4, 5

Now, let's say 2 is unschdulable. It puts 2 back and picks up 1 again, because it is at the head of the queue. The queue will be:

queue: 2, 3, 4, 5.

And the same sequence will happen again. Basically, 3, 4, 5 will never even get a chance to be scheduled.

The existing queue algorithm puts 1 at the end of the queue after it is tried. So, other pods will get a chance to be scheduled.

@bsalamat Thanks for this detailed reply :)
**But for your scenario, I would say 3, 4, 5 will still get chances to be scheduled.**
And this is **verified** in https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/83834, so you can see even after this fix, there are still some cut in line rate (1~10%).
So, after berifly checked our code, the true story seems like below, could you please double check it?
It mainly benefits from the unschedulable queue (and the backoff queue can also help some):
https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/f7091992c04e2d4f16f6b462d4a711e5b9eb0f22/pkg/scheduler/factory.go#L667-L679

So even after this PR, your scenario seems still behavior like:
**Init:**
active queue: 1, 2, 3, 4, 5

**1 failed and scheduling 2:**
active queue: 3, 4, 5
unschedulable queue: 1

**2 failed and scheduling 3:**
active queue: 4, 5
unschedulable queue: 1, 2

**3 failed and scheduling 4:**
active queue: 5
unschedulable queue: 1, 2, 3
etc.

So 3, 4, 5 will still get chances to be scheduled as **tested** (if there are not too frequent events in the cluster to move the unschedulable pods all the time immediately to active queue).
And this is what I have said to other approved reviewers before:

> You can think it is like the same thing as "high priority pod will not starve low priority pod" in current k8s scheduling, mentioned in wiki:
> https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/configuration/pod-priority-preemption/#effect-of-pod-priority-on-scheduling-order
> > As a result, the higher priority Pod may be scheduled sooner than Pods with lower priority if its scheduling requirements are met. If such Pod cannot be scheduled, scheduler will continue and tries to schedule other lower priority Pods.
> 

> The orignal UT makes **extreme corner cases** that failed old Pods always immediately requeued (without the fact that we can benefit from our great features: backoff and unscheduled queues). It is not realistic, so I removed it.
> 
> In another word, this PR **sacrifices the toleration for extreme case**, i.e. too frequent events, to **achieve the near FIFO scheduling behaiour which user really get benefits in most cases.**
> 


**And let's go back to the original interesting topic. I knew that:**
> It is already a FIFO for the pods that have never been tried before (and have the same priority).

But the PR is to make it **also FIFO for the tried pods**. This is especially important for a resource tight cluster, i.e. the cluster has pending pods in most of the time, this is very common in expensive GPU clusters.
You can see others also meet the similar issue: https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/83834#issuecomment-542684062

Another simple example is that:
Given 2 same pending pods A and B, but A is submitted 1 year ago, B is submitted 1 hour ago. Currently, A and B both failed to schedule, how would you plan to prioritize them in future?
If we plan to schedule B before A, what is the benefit?
Why not schedule A before B to align users' expectation?

@yqwang-ms the scenario that I described does not happen with 5 pods because the scheduler has a default 10 second backof mechanism. If you have a large number of unschedulable pods, the scenario that I described will happen. Regardless, that example shows why sorting by creation time is not fair.

But I tested 400 unscheduled pods that will not starve newer pods. Is it enough?

And regardless this specific PR, we can see we still have large space to improve the queuing policy fairness for users. Can we leverage unscheduled queue to be more fair? Or do you already think that current existing policy is fair enough？

BTW, this PR is most helpful when there are many unscheduled pods of the same priority, 1) gives them an **order/subpriority** that align with pod pending time. But under the same case, 2) you say it may starve newer pods.

I think 1) and 2) are 2 different questions, if we reach an agreement on 1), we can forcus on fix 2), instead of close both 1) and 2) immediately.

For 2), a preliminary idea is that, we can improve this PR to make sure that every Pods will be scheduled in a user specified (scheduling cycles/pending pods) rate.

@yqwang-ms   If there are a large number of unschedulable  pods created long time ago in the cluster, the new pod will wait for a long time.  I think It's unfair that the old unschedulable  pod tries to schedule many times, but the new pod of the same priority  keeps waiting.

@denkensk please tested it. In my test, 400 unschedulable pods created long time ago in the cluster, the new pod will be scheduled to a node within 10s. 

The unschedulable pods are already **determined** to be failed, so they are **suppressed** within the **unschedulable queue**, so newer pods will still get large chances to schedule (to be the head of active queue, since old pods are all **suppressed**, and some in backing off).

The interesting part is that, before this PR, someone (like me and our users) think it is unfair to old pods, and after this PR, someone (like you) think it is unfair to new pods.

So maybe existing policy and the policy after this PR are both unfair, maybe we need a trade off between new pods and old pods, as our default queuing policy.

Should this be added as a separate variable instead of overriding the time when the pod was added to the scheduling queue ? And how would the new logic prioritize between a pod1 that was added to the scheduling queue `n` seconds ago vs a pod2 that was tried scheduling `x` seconds ago, but  was added to the scheduling queue later (`n` > `x`) ?

1. This PR does not intend to make the field `Timestamp` better, I just make the comment more clear.

https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/e64be696d610c0063902c68422556730ed43c785/pkg/scheduler/internal/queue/scheduling_queue.go#L214-L215

So for your question, if pod1 has the same priority with pod2, the newer created Pod will be lower prioritized to scheduler.
